AI Chatbot Framework

A self-hosted AI agent for everyone on your team.
Each person gets an assistant with its own private computer, files, skills, app connections and scheduled tasks.

Quick start · Features · Deploy · Configuration · Architecture · Contributing

![AI Chatbot Framework home screen: chats, projects, files, skills, tasks, connections and personal apps in the sidebar, and the message box in the middle](docs/screenshots/home.webp) > **Version 2.** AI Chatbot Framework used to be an intent/entity NLU chatbot builder. Version 2 rebuilds it > as an agent. The old code is in the git history. ## Why Most agent tools are built for developers. This one is built for people who just want work done: they type what they need, and the agent reads their files, runs code, uses their apps and remembers how they like things. You run it on your own server, with the model of your choice, and every user's work stays in their own locked-down sandbox. ## Features - **Any model.** Claude by default; OpenAI, Ollama, OpenRouter, vLLM, LiteLLM or any other [LangChain](https://python.langchain.com) chat provider. Users can bring their own key. - **A private computer per user.** One Docker sandbox with a persistent `/workspace`, resource limits and no Linux capabilities. Commands and local MCP servers run there. - **A small, fast agent loop.** Four tools (`read`, `write`, `edit`, `bash`), parallel tool calls, background commands, context compaction, and **steering**: type while the agent works and it picks your message up without stopping. - **Sub-agents.** The agent splits a big job into parts and runs helpers side by side, each with a fresh context and its own model. You can watch each one work. - **Memory in plain files.** `context.md` (about you) and `memory.md` (what the agent remembers) are files the agent reads every turn and edits itself. Every few messages a background pass updates memory and skills from the chat. - **Skills.** The open Agent Skills format (`skills//SKILL.md`). Upload one, let the agent write one, or type `/` in a chat to pick one. Eleven come built in, from `pdf` and `cited-research` to `council-of-llms` and `personal-assistant`. - **App connections (MCP).** Local servers run in the sandbox; remote servers sign in with OAuth. One-click setup for Linear, Notion, Jira, Sentry, Stripe and more. - **Personal apps.** The agent can build small apps for you, like a daily **Cockpit** or a grocery list, that show up in the sidebar. Each app has its own chat in a panel on its right: ask for a change there and watch the app update as the agent works. Chat replies can include charts, tabs and buttons too. - **Projects and scheduled tasks.** Group chats under shared instructions and a folder. Run a prompt "every weekday at 08:00" or once "tomorrow at 17:00"; each run becomes a chat, on the model you pick for the task (a small local one is enough for many background jobs). - **Files and artifacts.** Attach files to a message; each chat lists the files it used and made; documents the agent writes open rendered beside the chat. - **Open protocol.** The chat speaks the [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com) over WebSocket, so editors and your own apps can talk to the agent too. - **Built to scale.** Stateless app processes behind Caddy, with PostgreSQL and Redis. Add or remove processes at any time. - **A calm interface.** Keyboard-first (⌘K, shortcuts), dark and light themes, works on a phone and installs as an app (PWA). Every feature in detail: [docs/features.md](docs/features.md). ## Screenshots | Steering while it works | Skills | Connections (OAuth) | |---|---|---| | ![Steering: a message queued while the agent works](docs/screenshots/e2e/04-steering-queued.png) | ![Skills page](docs/screenshots/e2e/07-skills.png) | ![Connections page with a connected app](docs/screenshots/e2e/09-connections-connected.png) | | **Files** | **Command menu (⌘K)** | **Phone, light theme** | | ![Files page](docs/screenshots/e2e/06-files.png) | ![Command menu](docs/screenshots/e2e/15-command-menu.png) | ![Chat on a phone in light theme](docs/screenshots/e2e/14-phone-light-chat.png) | | **Cockpit app** | **Sub-agents** | **Charts in a personal app** | | ![Cockpit personal app](docs/screenshots/e2e/41-app-cockpit-moved.png) | ![Sub-agents working in parallel](docs/screenshots/e2e/09-sub-agents-working.png) | ![Personal app with charts](docs/screenshots/e2e/52-app-charts.png) | The end-to-end tests take these screenshots on every run ([`docs/screenshots/e2e/`](docs/screenshots/e2e)). ## Quick start Try it on your machine with Docker. A scripted fake model answers, so you don't need an API key: ```sh git clone https://github.com/alfredfrancis/ai-chatbot-framework.git cd ai-chatbot-framework docker compose -f docker-compose.dev.yml up --build # or: make up-dev ``` Open http://localhost:5173 and create an account. Try `run: ls` or `show system` in a chat. To use a real model: ```sh ACF_LLM_BASE_URL= ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... make up-dev ```
Ports, database and running without Docker The web app is on :5173 and the API on :8000 (API only; use 5173). Both reload when you save. PostgreSQL is on host port 55432 (`postgresql://acf:acf@localhost:55432/acf`). If a port is taken, set `ACF_DEV_WEB_PORT`, `ACF_DEV_API_PORT` or `ACF_DEV_DB_PORT`. Agents run in real sandboxes. Without Docker, `make setup && make dev` runs the same thing on your machine (set `ACF_SANDBOX=local`; it is **not isolated**, so use it for development only).
## Deploy On a server with Docker and a domain pointing at it: ```sh git clone https://github.com/alfredfrancis/ai-chatbot-framework.git && cd ai-chatbot-framework cp .env.example .env # set ACF_DOMAIN, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, ACF_SECRET_KEY and a model key # prepare the host first: gVisor, user-namespace remapping, sandbox firewall (deploy/README.md) docker compose up -d # or: make up ``` > [!IMPORTANT] > Set up the host as described in [deploy/README.md](deploy/README.md) before going public. **Your account.** Set `ACF_ADMIN_EMAIL` and `ACF_ADMIN_PASSWORD` in `.env` to create your account at startup; sign-ups are then closed unless `ACF_ALLOW_SIGNUP=true`. Without them, open `https://`, create the first account, then set `ACF_ALLOW_SIGNUP=false`. **HTTPS.** [Caddy](https://caddyserver.com) gets and renews the certificate; ports 80 and 443 must be open. To use other host ports, set `ACF_HTTP_PORT` / `ACF_HTTPS_PORT` (e.g. `127.0.0.1:8088` behind a tunnel or another proxy). When that tunnel or proxy terminates HTTPS (e.g. Cloudflare Tunnel), also set `ACF_CADDY_ADDRESS=:80` so Caddy serves plain HTTP. Browsers only offer to install the web app as an app over HTTPS (or on `localhost`). **Images.** The stack pulls published images (`ACF_REGISTRY` / `ACF_VERSION` in `.env`), by default the version of the checkout you run it from. To build from source instead, run `docker compose up -d --build`. Versions and upgrades: [docs/releasing.md](docs/releasing.md). **Data.** PostgreSQL runs in its own container (volume `postgres-data`); workspaces live in `./data`, or `ACF_DATA_PATH`. Back up both. Logs are rotated and the app has health checks: `/api/health` is liveness (the process answers) and `/api/health/ready` is readiness (200 with `{"db":"ok","bus":"ok"}` when the database and, with `ACF_REDIS_URL`, Redis answer within 2 s; 503 otherwise). Point a load balancer or a Kubernetes readiness probe at the ready route and a liveness probe at the live one. **Security.** Each user gets one sandbox container. The app runs as a non-root user and never touches the Docker socket: a small proxy (`docker-proxy`) holds it and allows only sandbox containers with fixed, locked-down settings. Sandboxes run under gVisor, as a non-root user, on their own network, behind an egress firewall on the host. ### Scaling Run state is shared through Redis, so you can run as many app processes as you like and add or remove them at any time: ```sh docker compose up -d --scale app=3 ``` Caddy spreads requests and chat connections over them and picks up new ones within seconds. Any process serves any chat; each user still has one sandbox and one workspace. A stopping process lets its running agents finish first (`ACF_SHUTDOWN_GRACE`, default 20 s), and its clients reconnect to another one. A crashed process frees its chats after `ACF_BUS_TTL` (30 s). Taking a stopping process out of the rotation is the orchestrator's job: the process closes its listening socket when SIGTERM arrives, before its readiness check could report anything. With compose, Caddy looks up the app processes every 5 s and sends a request that a stopping process refuses to another one. On Kubernetes, give the app container a `preStop` hook that sleeps a few seconds (`sleep 5`), so the pod is removed from the Service's endpoints before SIGTERM arrives, and set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` above that sleep plus `ACF_SHUTDOWN_GRACE` (for example 40). Across several machines, every app process needs the same PostgreSQL, Redis and Docker proxy, and the data folder at the same path (shared storage), because sandboxes mount workspaces from the Docker host. Details: [architecture](docs/architecture.md#several-app-processes-backendacfbuspy). Upgrades migrate the database first: the `migrate` service runs `acf-migrate` and the app starts once it has finished. App processes also migrate when they start (`ACF_MIGRATE_ON_START`, default `true`), and processes that start together take turns on the schema. Where a deploy tool runs migrations as their own step (a Kubernetes Job or a Helm hook), run `acf-migrate` there and set `ACF_MIGRATE_ON_START=false` on the app, which then refuses to start on an older schema. Give the Job the app's `ACF_DB_URL` and `ACF_SECRET_KEY`: migrations can encrypt and decrypt stored secrets, and without the key `acf-migrate` stops with a message and leaves the database as it was. It never makes a key of its own, which the app wouldn't have; a `secret.key` file already in `ACF_DATA_DIR` (a local install) is used. During a rolling deploy the previous version's processes keep running, and restart or scale up, on the new schema. A process that finds a schema revision it doesn't know logs a warning naming both revisions and starts without migrating. That is safe only because migrations are expand/contract: each release's migrations keep the previous release working. Add tables, and columns that are nullable or have a server default, in one release; drop or rename what the code no longer uses in a later release. ## Configuration Environment variables. Users choose models in **Settings → Models**: their own key and address per provider, which models are on in the chat's model picker, a token window per model, and a default model and effort. Each chat can switch model and effort from its message box. | Variable | Default | Meaning | |---|---|---| | `ACF_LLM_PROVIDER` | `anthropic` | Any LangChain provider id: `anthropic`, `openai`, `ollama`, `google_genai`, … | | `ACF_LLM_PROVIDERS` | providers that take an API key | Providers users may choose (comma-separated, `*` = any). The server's own is always allowed | | `ACF_LLM_MODEL` | `claude-opus-5-5` / `gpt-4.1-mini` | Default model | | `ACF_MODELS_FILE` | built-in list | JSON list of the models users can pick, with their effort levels, default effort and token window (see below) | | `ACF_CUSTOM_MODELS` | `true` | Users may add models of their own; `false` limits everyone to the models list | | `ACF_LLM_API_KEY` | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` / `OPENAI_API_KEY` | Server-wide key, used by every user without their own. Only sent to the server's provider and `ACF_LLM_BASE_URL` | | `ACF_SECRET_KEY` | generated in `ACF_DATA_DIR/secret.key` | Encrypts API keys, MCP configs and OAuth tokens in the database. Required by the production stack | | `ACF_LLM_BASE_URL` | provider default | e.g. `http://localhost:11434/v1` with `openai` for Ollama | | `ACF_MAX_AGENT_STEPS` | `40` | Model calls per message (and per sub-agent) | | `ACF_SUBAGENTS` | `8` | Sub-agents of one run working at the same time; more wait their turn (`0` = no sub-agents) | | `ACF_SUBAGENT_FAST_MODEL` | provider's small model | The model a sub-agent gets when the agent asks for `fast` (Claude: `claude-haiku-5-5`, OpenAI: `gpt-4.1-mini`, others: the user's model) | | `ACF_COMPACT_TOKENS` / `ACF_COMPACT_KEEP_TOKENS` | `120000` / `20000` | When to summarise old messages, and how much recent history to keep. A model with a token window set (models file or the user's settings) compacts at 80% of that window instead | | `ACF_CONTEXT_WINDOW` | model's own | Context window size (tokens) for the chat's context meter when the model has no token window set; default comes from LangChain's model profile, `128000` if unknown | | `ACF_MEMORY_LIMIT` | `4000` | Characters of `memory.md` (it goes into every prompt); the agent's writes past it are refused | | `ACF_REVIEW_INTERVAL` | `10` | User messages per chat between background reviews that update memory and skills (`0` = off) | | `ACF_AUTO_TITLES` | `true` | After a chat's first reply, the chat's model names it in a few words (`false`: chats keep their first message as title) | | `ACF_SKILL_ARCHIVE_DAYS` | `30` | Skills not read for this many days move to `skills/.archive/` (`0` = never; `pinned: true` in a skill's frontmatter keeps it) | | `ACF_DB_URL` | SQLite in `ACF_DATA_DIR` | Database. The Docker stacks use PostgreSQL (`postgresql://user:pass@host/db`) | | `ACF_MIGRATE_ON_START` | `true` | Each app process brings the database schema up to date as it starts. `false`: run `acf-migrate` first (a Kubernetes Job, say), and a process that finds an older schema exits with an error naming it | | `ACF_DATA_DIR` | `./data` | Workspaces (and the SQLite file when no `ACF_DB_URL` is set) | | `ACF_ADMIN_EMAIL` / `ACF_ADMIN_PASSWORD` | – | Main account, created at startup; its password is reset to this value (and its sessions signed out) when it changes | | `ACF_ADMIN_NAME` | email name | Display name for the main account | | `ACF_ALLOW_SIGNUP` | `true`, `false` if `ACF_ADMIN_EMAIL` is set | Open sign-ups. When `false`, the first account can still be created on an empty server | | `ACF_COOKIE_SECURE` | `false` | `true` behind HTTPS | | `ACF_SANDBOX` | `docker` | `docker`, `local` for development (**not isolated**), or your own adapter as `package.module:Class` (see [architecture](docs/architecture.md#sandboxes-backendacfsandboxpy)). Upgrading an adapter from 2.0.0-beta.1 or earlier: rename its `exec` method to `run`; the app refuses to start with one that still defines `exec` | | `ACF_SANDBOX_IMAGE` | `acf-sandbox:latest` | Sandbox image | | `ACF_SANDBOX_NETWORK` | `acf-sandbox` | Created when missing, with traffic between sandboxes off. `none` cuts sandboxes off from the internet | | `ACF_SANDBOX_BRIDGE` | `acf-sbx0` | Interface name of that network (the egress firewall matches it) | | `ACF_SANDBOX_RUNTIME` | – (`runsc` in the production stack) | Container runtime, e.g. `runsc` for gVisor | | `ACF_SANDBOX_MEMORY` / `_CPUS` | `1g` / `1` | Limits per sandbox | | `ACF_SANDBOX_IDLE_MINUTES` | `30` | Stop a sandbox no one has used for this long; it starts again, files intact, on the next command. `0` never stops one | | `ACF_SANDBOX_HOST_DATA_DIR` | – | Host path of the data dir when the app itself runs in Docker | | `ACF_MCP_PRESETS_FILE` | – | JSON list of extra one-click apps for the Connections page (see below) | | `ACF_REDIS_URL` | – (set in the production stack) | Redis for run state shared between app processes. Needed for more than one process; unset keeps it in memory | | `ACF_REDIS_PREFIX` | `acf` | Key prefix, to share one Redis between deployments | | `ACF_BUS_TTL` | `30` | Seconds before a dead process's chats, locks and background commands are freed | | `ACF_SHUTDOWN_GRACE` | `20` | Seconds a stopping process gives its running agents to finish | | `ACF_LOG_FORMAT` | `text` | `json` writes one JSON object per line to stderr (`ts`, `level`, `logger`, `message`, plus `request_id`, `user_id`, `chat_id`, `run_id` and `task_id` where they apply, and `exc` for a traceback). A request keeps an incoming `X-Request-Id` (and returns it); a run is `run_id`, shared by its sub-agents. Message text and tool output are never logged, and key-like tokens are redacted. Inside a span, lines also carry `trace_id` and `span_id` | | `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` | – (off) | OpenTelemetry traces and metrics over OTLP/HTTP (protobuf) to this collector address, e.g. `http://otel-collector:4318`. `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT` / `..._METRICS_ENDPOINT` turn on one signal only. Unset, nothing is exported and nothing is measured. The other standard `OTEL_*` variables apply (`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS`, `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER`, `OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL`, `OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES`, `OTEL_SDK_DISABLED`…). Spans: each HTTP request (by route), `acf.run`, `acf.turn`, `acf.llm`, `acf.tool`, `acf.sandbox.exec`, `acf.follow`. Metrics: `acf.runs.active`, `acf.run.duration`, `acf.tool.calls`, `acf.sandbox.start.duration`, `acf.llm.tokens`, `acf.acp.connections`. No message text, tool arguments, commands or query strings are recorded, and no metric has a per-user label | | `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` | `acf` | The service name on exported traces and metrics | ### Models The models users can pick come from a built-in list (Claude Opus/Sonnet/Haiku/Fable, GPT-5, GPT-5 mini, GPT-4.1 mini), or from `ACF_MODELS_FILE`, which replaces it: ```json [ {"provider": "anthropic", "id": "claude-opus-5-5", "name": "Claude Opus 5.5", "efforts": ["low", "medium", "high", "max"], "effort": "medium", "context_window": 200000, "max_context_window": 1000000}, {"provider": "openai", "id": "gpt-5", "efforts": ["minimal", "low", "medium", "high"], "effort": "medium"} ] ``` `efforts` are the effort levels the model accepts (left out: no effort setting) and `effort` the default; effort goes to Claude as `output_config.effort` and to OpenAI as `reasoning_effort`. `context_window` is the token window the context meter and compaction use (left out: the model's own); users may set their own up to `max_context_window`. Only models of providers in `ACF_LLM_PROVIDERS` are offered. In a user's list, models whose provider has a key (theirs, or the server's for the server's own provider) start out on. Other LangChain providers need their package installed (`pip install langchain-ollama`, …). **A local model for background jobs.** `docker-compose.withllm.yml` adds llama.cpp's `llama-server` with Qwen3.5 4B, sized for a Raspberry Pi 5 with 8 GB, with prompt caching. Pick it as a task's model so hourly jobs run on your own hardware: [docs/local-model.md](docs/local-model.md). ### App connections (MCP) Add, edit, turn off or delete connections from the form on the **Connections** page. Switch to **JSON** there to edit the whole configuration directly (same format as Claude Desktop; needed for extra keys like `oauth`, which the form keeps but doesn't edit). The API equivalents are `PUT`/`DELETE /api/mcp/servers/{name}` and `PUT /api/mcp/config`. ```json { "mcpServers": { "filesystem": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/workspace"] }, "linear": { "url": "https://mcp.linear.app/mcp" }, "internal": { "url": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp", "headers": { "X-Api-Key": "…" } }, "github": { "url": "https://api.example.com/mcp", "oauth": { "client_id": "…", "scopes": ["repo"] } } } } ``` `oauth.authorize_params` adds parameters to the provider's sign-in URL. Google, for example, only issues a refresh token with `{ "access_type": "offline", "prompt": "consent" }`; without one the connection ends when the access token expires. **Popular apps.** The Connections page lists remote MCP servers that support OAuth dynamic client registration — Linear, Notion, Jira & Confluence, Sentry, monday.com, Canva, Intercom, Stripe, Vercel and Hugging Face. **Connect** writes the entry into your configuration; **Sign in** does the rest, no API key needed. To add your own (or override a built-in one by `id`), point `ACF_MCP_PRESETS_FILE` at a JSON file: ```json [{ "id": "acme", "name": "Acme", "description": "Tickets and docs", "url": "https://mcp.acme.com/mcp" }] ``` ### Skills A skill is a folder with a `SKILL.md`: ```markdown --- name: weekly-report description: Write the weekly sales report. Use when asked for the weekly report. --- # Weekly report 1. Run `python skills/weekly-report/make.py data/sales.csv` 2. … ``` Upload it as a `.zip` (or just the `SKILL.md`) on the Skills page, or ask the agent to create one — every workspace starts with a `skill-creator` skill that teaches it how, plus a few general skills (`backend/acf/builtin_skills/`). Each built-in skill is added once; one you delete stays deleted. ### Editors and external apps (ACP) The agent is reachable over the [Agent Client Protocol](https://agentclientprotocol.com): JSON-RPC 2.0, one message per WebSocket text frame, at `ws(s):///api/acp`. The web chat uses the same endpoint (with its session cookie, same origin only). Other clients authenticate with `Authorization: Bearer `, using the access token from **Settings → External apps**. External access is off until a token is created; the token is shown once, stored hashed, and can be replaced or revoked at any time. Supported: `initialize`, `session/new`, `session/load` (replays the history, then follows a running agent), `session/list`, `session/prompt` (text, resource links and embedded text resources), `session/cancel` and `session/set_config_option`: `session/new` and `session/load` return the chat's `configOptions`, a `model` select (the user's models that are on) and, for models that have one, an `effort` select (`thought_level`). A resource link to `file:///workspace/` is an attached workspace file: `session/load` replays it as a `resource_link` chunk after the message's text (upload the file first with `POST /api/files`, `keep=true`). Each session is a chat in the web app. Updates are `user_message_chunk`, `agent_message_chunk` and `agent_thought_chunk` (streamed as the model writes; chunks of one message share `_meta.acf.messageId`), `tool_call`, `tool_call_update` and `session_info_update`. A `session/prompt` sent while the agent works is a steering message; its response arrives when the run ends. Extras live under `_acf/` (`_acf/notice`, `_acf/turn_end`, `_acf/turn_start` when a finished background command wakes the agent) and `_meta.acf`, which other clients can ignore. The agent uses its own sandbox and connections, so `cwd` and `mcpServers` from the client are ignored. Clients that start agents as a subprocess over stdio (most editors) can use the bridge: ```sh ACF_ACP_TOKEN=acp_… python -m acf.acp_bridge --url wss://agent.example.com/api/acp ``` ## Contributing Contributions are welcome. Read [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) first: it covers the layout, the rules (every feature is tested end to end, including the UI) and the workflow. The design of the agent loop is in [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md). ```sh make setup # Python venv + npm install make sandbox-image # or set ACF_SANDBOX=local make dev # API :8000 + web :5173 make test # backend tests (Docker tests run when a daemon is available) make e2e # Playwright end-to-end tests (writes docs/screenshots/e2e) make e2e-docker # the same with real Docker sandboxes (what CI runs) make lint ``` Tests never call a real model: `backend/tests/fakes/` has a scripted model server (Anthropic and OpenAI APIs), a dependency-free stdio MCP server and an OAuth-protected HTTP MCP server. Design tokens live in `design/tokens.json` (mirroring the design system in Claude Design); `cd frontend && npm run tokens` regenerates `src/tokens.css`. ## Known limitations - Sandboxes refuse to start when the workspace belongs to root: run the app as a normal user. - No per-user quotas yet (model spend, disk, number of sandboxes), and no rate limiting on sign-in. ## License MIT.
